clue.text: Even more inflammable than Blake's but less fearful

definitions.text: Even more inflammable than Blake's but less fearful

parts.words: Even more inflammable than Blake's but less fearful
parts.note: Blake's Tyger is 'burning bright' with 'fearful symmetry'; a sham big cat made of something that catches fire easily burns more readily and frightens nobody

explanation.surface: A literary comparison with Blake's famous poem about a fierce, blazing beast.
explanation.walkthrough: William Blake's poem 'The Tyger' begins 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright' and speaks of its 'fearful symmetry'. The clue imagines a literal flimsy version that would burn even better but scare no one.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper tiger is a threat that looks fierce but is powerless, so it is less fearful than the real beast.

clue.text: Chooses tools

definitions.meaning: pointed implements for breaking ground or ice

explanation.definitionFit: To pick is to select, and picks are also pointed digging implements like the pickaxe.

clue.text: Puts forward something in sterling's favour?

definitions.meaning: pro means in favour of, and sterling is counted in pounds, so a split reading backs the currency

explanation.definitionFit: To propound is to propose an idea; read as two parts it says 'for the pound', supporting British currency.

clue.text: Exotic flowers to be had for a song

definitions.text: Exotic flowers to be had for a song

parts.words: Exotic flowers to be had for a song
parts.note: 'for a song' seems to mean cheaply, but these foreign blooms are literally the title of a famous First World War ballad about northern France

explanation.surface: Foreign blooms going cheap at the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a song' usually means very cheaply; here the flowers are the title of a 1916 popular song set in a region of northern France.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names roses from a French region and is also the title of a well-known wartime ballad.

clue.text: True of one who would be never at a loss

definitions.text: True of one who would be never at a loss

parts.words: True of one who would be never at a loss
parts.note: someone holding a policy is compensated after any mishap, so in money terms never ends up out of pocket

explanation.surface: A description of a person who always has an answer ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never at a loss' suggests someone quick-witted; the clue means someone whose losses are always covered by a policy.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with cover from an underwriter is repaid for damage or theft, so suffers no financial loss.

clue.text: Foiled Martext ?

parts.note: Sir Oliver Martext is the vicar in As You Like It; split as 'mar text', a name whose aim is foiled describes writing that has been corrected rather than spoiled

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean minor character, Sir Oliver Martext, being thwarted.
explanation.walkthrough: Martext is the hedge-priest in Shakespeare's As You Like It; read as 'mar text', to foil him is to put a text right instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A text that is emended has had its errors corrected, the opposite of being marred.

clue.text: Employments in U.S. essential industries

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the words U.S. essential industries

explanation.surface: A remark about the jobs found in key American industries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the hidden word, which runs across the opening letters of 'U.S. essential'.
explanation.definitionFit: Uses are applications or employments of something, as in putting a tool to good employment.

clue.text: Dog that behaves like a cat to one ?

definitions.text: Dog that behaves like a cat to one

parts.words: Dog that behaves like a cat to one
parts.note: an angry cat spits at you, and this breed's name sounds like that verb, so a dog of this type seems to act like a cat

explanation.surface: A puzzling dog that acts like a cat towards someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The breed's name sounds like 'spits', what a hostile cat does to a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The spitz is a family of dog breeds with pointed muzzles and curled tails, such as the Pomeranian.

clue.text: Drink for Eve and the hobo

definitions.meaning: Eve is short for evening, so a drink taken at the end of the day
a vagrant; the Australian swagman who turned up at sundown for food and shelter

explanation.definitionFit: A sundowner is an evening drink taken at sunset, and in Australian slang a tramp who arrives at a homestead at nightfall.

clue.text: Libra ascendant ?

parts.note: Libra is the sign of the scales, and an ascendant sign is the one in control, so the scales would be in control

explanation.surface: An astrological note that Libra is the rising sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ascendant' is an astrology term, but it also means dominant; Libra is the scales, so balance is in power.
explanation.definitionFit: The balance of power is the equilibrium between rival nations, read here as the scales holding sway.

clue.text: Mongrels nought may come between

definitions.meaning: in noughts and ... an O can be placed between two X marks

explanation.definitionFit: Crossbreeds are mixed-breed animals, and in the game of noughts and crosses an O may be placed between two X marks.

clue.text: What euphoria when a kinsman is seen right off' !

indicators.note: seen off means removed, so the letter for right is taken away from the kinsman

parts.note: a kinsman is a relation by blood

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the joy felt when a relative finally leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is a feeling of great happiness, the same intense joy as euphoria.

clue.text: For op, no dress required, and the programme is paid for

indicators.note: the letters of op and no dress are needed in a new order, so the word asks for them to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An operation needs no special clothing, and a sponsor funds the broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'required' signals rearranging OP NO DRESS. 'op' is a surgical operation in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponsored broadcast is one whose cost is met by an advertiser, so it is funded by someone else.

clue.text: In a wizard place of confusion and battle

indicators.note: letters in confusion are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: Oz is the land ruled by the Wizard in L. Frank Baum's story

explanation.surface: A wizard's realm full of chaos and fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confusion' signals rearranging IN, A and OZ (the Wizard's land).
explanation.definitionFit: Anzio in Italy was the site of a major Allied landing and battle in 1944.

clue.text: Where visitors are required to turn down their transistors ?

definitions.text: Where visitors are required to turn down their transistors

parts.words: Where visitors are required to turn down their transistors
parts.note: split the place name as a prohibition followed by the musical marking for very loud, so loud radio playing is forbidden there

explanation.surface: A quiet resort that asks guests to keep their radios down.
explanation.walkthrough: The town splits as BAN + FF, where ff (fortissimo) is the musical mark for very loud: loud music banned.
explanation.definitionFit: Banff is a resort town, in Scotland and in Canada, so a place visitors go.

clue.text: Sir Andrew thought he had it as strong as any man in Illyria

definitions.text: Sir Andrew thought he had it as strong as any man in Illyria

parts.words: Sir Andrew thought he had it as strong as any man in Illyria
parts.note: in Twelfth Night Sir Andrew Aguecheek boasts of a dance move he can perform as well as anyone in Illyria

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's foolish knight boasting of a skill.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night (Act 1 Scene 3) Sir Andrew says he has the back-trick 'simply as strong as any man in Illyria'.
explanation.definitionFit: A back-trick is a backwards caper in dancing, the step the knight brags about.

clue.text: Something off Holmes's fee ?

parts.note: an amount taken off a bill, and also the reasoning method the famous detective is known for

explanation.surface: A discount on the detective's charges.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both a reduction in a fee and the logical method Sherlock Holmes uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A deduction is a subtraction from a sum and also reasoning from evidence, the detective's trademark.

clue.text: Healthy to be out with the hounds

definitions.meaning: in good condition, fit and well

definitions.text: to be out with the hounds
definitions.meaning: fox hunters wear red coats called pink, so riders out hunting are dressed in that colour

explanation.definitionFit: Being in fine fettle is an idiom for good health, and fox hunters wear red coats called hunting pink.

clue.text: Players with just one lot of admission money make hits

parts.note: the players in a play are its cast
I is the Roman numeral one
the gate is the total taken from spectators paying to enter

explanation.surface: A theatre company earning one round of ticket money produces successes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make hits' reads as staging successful shows, but it means to strike or punish. 'just' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to punish severely, originally by beating, so to deal blows.

clue.text: . Where innocence is bliss

parts.note: a play on 'ignorance is bliss': an idealised pastoral land of simple, unspoiled happiness

explanation.surface: A twist on the saying that ignorance is bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'ignorance is bliss' is changed to describe the classical paradise of innocent shepherds.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcadia is the idealised rustic paradise of Greek and Renaissance poetry, a place of simple contentment.

clue.text: Always a weighty side

parts.note: ever means always
a ton is a great weight

explanation.surface: A team that is always heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'side' is a sports team; EVERTON is a Liverpool football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is an English football club, and a team is called a side in British usage.

clue.text: Fisher hunted

parts.note: a river animal that catches fish and was formerly pursued with hounds

explanation.definitionFit: The otter is an aquatic mammal that lives on fish and was hunted with otterhounds in Britain.

clue.text: A 20 booked

parts.note: 20 across is a river-dwelling fish-eater; this one is the hero of a famous book by Henry Williamson

explanation.definitionFit: Tarka is the animal hero of Henry Williamson's novel about a Devon river creature, so one put in a book.

clue.text: Wainside's delirious

definitions.meaning: a wain is a farm wagon; its side rails, read as 'wainsides is'
talking wildly, as someone who is delirious does

explanation.definitionFit: Raves are the side rails of a wagon or cart, and a person who raves talks wildly as if delirious.

clue.text: One side of London is noted for it

definitions.text: One side of London is noted for it

parts.words: One side of London is noted for it
parts.note: Cheapside is a historic street in the City of London, so 'one side' is that street name's first part plus a quality

explanation.surface: A remark that one part of the capital is known for low prices.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheapside is a street in the City of London; the clue treats its name as a 'side' known for being cheap.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inexpensive is the quality the first half of the London street name suggests.

clue.text: Neat painter

definitions.meaning: an old word for oxen or cattle
Philip Wilson ..., the English Impressionist artist

explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an old word for cattle, of which a young castrated bull is one, and Philip Wilson Steer was an English painter.

clue.text: Made an unwanted income from the vine. Dad

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of vine and Dad, worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone gets unwelcome earnings from Dad's grapevine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'income' looks like earnings but means coming in; 'from' signals rearranging VINE DAD.
explanation.definitionFit: To invade is to enter by force, so an unwelcome coming-in.

clue.text: Hempen rope for tug

parts.note: a strong rope by which one boat pulls another; 'tug' seems to be a pull but is the towing boat

explanation.definitionFit: A towline is the rope used to haul a vessel, as a tugboat does.

clue.text: X for O ?

parts.note: at the end of a letter X stands for one sign of affection and O for a hug; the clue asks what the X is

explanation.definitionFit: A cross at the end of a letter conventionally stands for a kiss, the O for a hug.

clue.text: He makes advances

parts.note: seems to be a flirt, but means someone who lends money against pledged goods

explanation.definitionFit: A pawnbroker lends money on the security of goods left with him, so he gives loans.
